summary: Austin-style breakfast tacos: warm corn tortillas with refried beans, roasted potato halves, tender scrambled eggs, salsa and minced cilantro and onion, about three bites each; serves 4 generously at 3 tacos each.
glance: soft warm corn tortillas and don't overfill
heated on a griddle, or microwaved in a damp towel for about 2 minutes
faq: What are the key principles of a breakfast taco?
Use good, soft, warm corn tortillas, and don't overfill them. A taco should be just about three bites of food; if you're hungry, make more tacos.
What goes in these vegetarian breakfast tacos?
Refried beans, oven-roasted halved small potatoes, tender scrambled eggs, fresh salsa (a smoky one is nice), minced cilantro and white onion, and hot sauce.
How do I warm the tortillas?
On a griddle, or wrap them in a clean, slightly dampened towel and microwave about two minutes until soft.
How do I make a vegan version?
Try butternut squash or tofu in place of the eggs.
Why Austin?
The author says Austin may be most famous for barbecue, but breakfast tacos seem a close second, and ask five Austinites for the best place and you'll get six opinions.

glance: 1 tablespoon red miso (boost to 2 or 3 tablespoons if you like)

summary: Pan-fried potato gnocchi with baby arugula and pecorino romano: boiled gnocchi fried in butter until crispy and brown on both sides, tossed with arugula for about 30 seconds and finished with shaved cheese; serves 4.
glance: 4 tablespoons, in a single layer over medium-high heat
faq: Why pan-fry gnocchi?
Frying them in butter makes the most of their texture. For pan-frying you want a little bit of density in the dumpling, which makes gnocchi that came out a bit heavy a good candidate.
How do you pan-fry gnocchi?

Boil according to your recipe, drain and cool. Melt the butter in a large pan over medium-high heat, add the gnocchi in a single layer, and fry until crispy and brown on one side, then flip. Drain off most of the butter.
When do I add the arugula?
After the gnocchi crisp up: add the arugula with 1/2 teaspoon of salt and toss until it just begins to wilt, maybe 30 seconds.
How do you get lighter gnocchi?
The author hasn't mastered ultra-light potato gnocchi. One tip from Paul Bertolli: when forking the gnocchi, dip the tines in flour before each one.
What toppings work?
Thinly shaved pecorino romano or parmigiano reggiano (a vegetable peeler works well), black pepper, flaky salt, and optionally toasted walnuts.

summary: Swiss chard, onion and Monterey Jack enchiladas baked 25 minutes in a cooked-down tomatillo salsa, loosely based on a Rick Bayless recipe; the chard stems go in too, and a single cup of broth keeps the sauce thick.
glance: 375°F for about 25 minutes, then broil a couple of minutes
1 1/2 pounds tomatillos pureed with garlic and jalapeno, reduced, then simmered 10 minutes
faq: Can you eat Swiss chard stems?

Yes. With chard, remove just the woodiest bit, chop the rest of the stem fairly small and give it enough time to cook; the author calls it a delicious, toothsome part of the vegetable and a big part of what made these enchiladas good.
How do you make the tomatillo sauce?

Puree garlic, jalapenos, tomatillos and 1 teaspoon salt, cook down in oil until about as thick as an Italian tomato sauce, stirring so it doesn't scorch, add a cup of broth and simmer 10 minutes, then stir in sour cream and adjust with salt and sugar.
What broth do I use?
A cup of bean cooking liquid if you cooked pinto beans from scratch, otherwise good vegetable broth. Bayless's recipe calls for two cups, but the author found that too loose, so this uses one.
How do I keep the chard from being gritty?
Rinse the leaves in a full bath of water at least twice, and rinse the stems thoroughly too, because gritty enchiladas are nasty.
How do you assemble the enchiladas?

Soften 12 tortillas wrapped in a moist towel in the microwave for 2 minutes, dip each in sauce, fill with about 1/4 cup of the chard-onion-cheese filling, roll, and pack seam-side down in a 9x13 casserole over a cup of sauce, then top with more sauce, cheese and parmesan and bake.
What do you serve with them?
Freshly made guacamole and refried beans. Leftover salsa also makes huevos ahogados.

summary: Boyikos (boyos de queso) are Sephardic cheese biscuits: a dough of 2 cups grated pecorino romano, oil, ice water and flour, rolled in more cheese, flattened to about 1 inch, pressed with a fork and baked at 400°F for about 15 minutes; makes about 4 dozen.
glance: 3 cups finely grated pecorino romano (2 in the dough, 1 for rolling)
faq: What are boyikos?
Little cheese biscuits or crackers that every good Sephardic grandmother makes: savory, crispy, flaky and cheesy. Names vary (boyos, boyos de rayo, boyos de queso), and each family has its own twist.
What cheese do you use?
Just about any hard grating cheese. Pecorino romano is the family tradition, but parmesan or even manchego work well.
How should the dough feel?
It holds together but is still somewhat soft, firm enough to hold a mark when pressed with fork tines. You might need a little more or less than 2 cups of flour.
How do you shape boyikos?

Take a piece of dough smaller than 2 teaspoons, form a ball, roll in the remaining cheese, then flatten on the baking sheet to about 1 inch across and 1/4 inch thick. Press each with fork tines for decoration.
How long do they bake?
About 15 minutes at 400°F, until golden brown but not real dark. Cool a couple of minutes, then move to a wire rack, and cool the cookie sheet before the next batch.
What do they go with?
The author says a martini never had a better companion; they're also great for potlucks.

olive oil, pomegranate molasses, dukkah, pickled shallot, cilantro
